questions.title: Does 'strict adherence' to La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G) implicitly require a human signature on cancellation notices?
questions.question_body: In *Williams v. GoAuto*, the Fifth Circuit affirmed that Louisiana's requirement for 'strict adherence' to insurance cancellation statutes does not mandate a signature on the certification notice sent by the premium finance company. The court noted the statute uses the word 'certifying' but doesn't explicitly say 'signed.' Given that previous cases like *Benitez v. Elsayed* criticized notices lacking signatures (even if not holding them fatal per se), how do courts generally determine when 'strict adherence' crosses the line from following the text to adding extra-statutory requirements? Is there a doctrinal test for when a missing formality renders a statutory certification invalid?

questions.title: How does the Fifth Circuit define 'receipt' under La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i) in the context of automated server-to-server communication?
questions.question_body: The opinion discusses whether GoAuto 'received' the cancellation request when its computer system automatically processed an email from APAC before any human employee saw it or stamped it. The court relied on Black's Law Dictionary definitions of 'receipt' involving taking possession. Does this ruling establish that digital 'possession' by a server counts as legal receipt even if no human agent has reviewed or acknowledged the document yet? How does this interact with the principle that an agent (the APAC employee stamping later) seemingly acted after the principal (GoAuto) had already effected the cancellation?

questions.title: Why did the Fifth Circuit decline to certify the questions of statutory interpretation to the Louisiana Supreme Court?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs argued that terms like 'certifying' and 'receipt' were undefined by the Louisiana Supreme Court and crucial to the state's insurance scheme, warranting certification. However, the Fifth Circuit denied this, citing *Jefferson v. Lead Indus. Ass'n*. Can someone explain the threshold for certification in diversity cases? Specifically, why does the mere absence of a state supreme court ruling on a specific term fail to meet the 'compelling reason' standard required by the Fifth Circuit?

questions.title: What is the legal significance of the timeline between automatic cancellation and the subsequent physical stamping of documents?
questions.question_body: The facts show that GoAuto's system cancelled policies immediately upon email receipt, while the physical paperwork was signed/stamped by an APAC employee hours later. The plaintiffs argued this sequence violated the statute. The court seemed to treat the electronic notice as sufficient pre-cancellation compliance. Does this imply that post-cancellation administrative formalities (like signing hard copies for files) are irrelevant to the validity of the cancellation itself, provided the electronic prerequisites were met first?

questions.title: Did the district court's alternative 'private carrier' theory impact the appellate court's reasoning or final holding?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that the district court had alternatively ruled that an APAC employee delivering papers fit the definition of a 'private carrier' under the statute, relying on an unpublished railroad case (*Huntley*). However, the Fifth Circuit explicitly stated they would not consider the validity of this definition because they resolved the case on email/electronic receipt grounds. Does leaving this issue unresolved create ambiguity for future cases where electronic transmission might fail, forcing reliance on physical delivery methods?

questions.title: How does this ruling affect breach of good faith claims when underlying statutory cancellation procedures are deemed compliant?
questions.question_body: The plaintiffs alleged breach of good faith and fair dealing based on improper cancellation procedures. Since the Fifth Circuit affirmed that GoAuto strictly adhered to La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G), does this automatically negate any bad faith claim as a matter of law in Louisiana? Or is it possible for an insurer to follow statutory technicalities perfectly but still act in bad faith due to other circumstances not covered by this specific procedural appeal?
